paper.title: The life-cycle and opportunities of migrants and natives in the Danish experience
paper.journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability statement (p. 15): "The data that has been used is confidential." No replication-code statement and no Statistics Denmark project number are given.

registers.name_in_paper: Danish administrative records collected from Statistics Denmark (Danmarks Statistik)

registers.role: linkage (parental relationships and age) and detection of cohabitation

registers.name_in_paper: Civil Registered Data (Central Person Register number)
registers.role: definition of residence; used to measure transit migration
mortality, used for the transit-migration check and the mortality-selection test

linkages: Individuals linked to their father and paternal grandfather through BEF-Befolkningen, so that each individual's genealogical tree spans three generations (patrilineal descent only).
All individuals linked to firms through an identification number (Danish register data).
Cohabiting partners detected from BEF-Befolkningen; partner's origin used in the assortative-mating check.

Country of origin of the first generation assigned with IE_TYPE (immigrant / descendant / person of Danish origin), OPR_LAND (country of origin, available from 2007 onward) and STATSB (country of citizenship) and then grouped by the World Bank GNI income classification of December 2020.

sample.universe: The entire resident population of Denmark, 1980-2021: 5,867,412 individuals in 2021 and 8,609,396 individuals over the whole period.
sample.unit_of_observation: Individual-year for the life-cycle analysis (Eq. 2); father-son (patrilineal) pair for the rank-rank and mechanism analyses (Eqs. 1, 3-7).
selection_rules: From the resident population, keep individuals whose parental relationships can be constructed from BEF: 4,298,683.
Keep males only (patrilineal descent): 2,228,504 male individuals.
Keep males for whom both the father and the paternal grandfather are identified (three-generation tree): 889,904.
Keep those with income information: 726,013 observations (life-cycle sample; about 3.1% immigrants); males aged at least 15 in 2021, i.e. born 2006 or before.

For the rank-rank and mechanism analyses: drop the first generation (grandfathers) and keep male individuals for whom the father is identified; use the average salary when father and son are both aged 35-40 inclusive (539,063 observations in Table 3).
For the Section 4 mechanism analysis: exclude sons who were born before the father's arrival in Denmark.
For the rank-rank regressions of Eq. (1): keep country-of-origin groups with 200 or more individuals.
Individuals of unknown origin (stateless citizens and people from broad geographical regions) are not considered in the econometric analysis.
sample.period: 1980-2021 (salary observed 1980-2019; year dummies 1981-2019; migration shares in Fig. 1 cover 1986-2019)
sample.n_observations: 726,013 (life-cycle analysis, Table 2); 539,063 (rank-rank and mechanism analysis, Table 3); 538,814 (entire-sample regressions in Tables 5 and 6)
sample.n_individuals: 8,609,396 residents over 1980-2021; 889,904 males with father and paternal grandfather identified

construction_notes: Salary is computed from LOENMV (taxable salary, fringe benefits, tax-free salary, anniversary and severance pay, value of stock options), deflated with 2019 as base year and converted to US dollars.
Observations with a salary of zero are included (about 8% in the second generation and about 17% in the third).
Robustness check uses total income = PERINDKIALT + LEJEV_EGEN_BOLIG, deflated to 2019 and converted to US dollars (footnote 13).
Ranks are built with ties assigned the average rank within the same homogeneous group, following Chetty et al. (2014).
For the rank-rank and mechanism analyses, income is the average salary when father and son are both aged 35-40 inclusive.
Education is HFPRIA, the normalized total number of months in the education system including compulsory elementary education.
Country-of-origin income groups follow the World Bank GNI classification reported at December 2020 (low, lower-middle, upper-middle, high income); the country list is Table A1 in the Appendix.
Measures based on few observations (minimum, maximum, medians, percentiles) are not permitted to be reported by Statistics Denmark.
In Table 3 the standard-deviation row printed for 'Foreigners' repeats the figures printed for 'Danes' (29,726.98 / 42,311.33 / 28.71), which appears to be a typesetting error in the paper.

claims.statement: Among father-son pairs of Danish origin, a one-unit increase in the father's income rank is associated with a 0.22 unit increase in the son's income rank (rank-rank slope of Eq. (1)).

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark administrative registers; salary variable LOENMV

definition.value: Rank of the mean income of the father in the Danish income distribution, built from the average salary over the years in which the father is aged 35-40; ties are assigned the average rank following Chetty et al. (2014).

timing.value: Average salary over the years in which the father is aged 35-40 inclusive

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark administrative registers; salary variable LOENMV

definition.value: Rank of the mean income of the son in the Danish income distribution, built from the average salary over the years in which the son is aged 35-40.

timing.value: Average salary over the years in which the son is aged 35-40 inclusive

units.value: son's income rank per unit of father's income rank (rank-rank slope)

magnitude.interpretation: The higher the slope, the lower the mobility of the sons with respect to their parents' position (p. 8).

estimand.target_population: Sons in Denmark with a Danes (individuals of Danish origin), observed at ages 35-40, whose fathers are also observed at ages 35-40.
estimand.time_horizon: Father and son each observed as the average salary over ages 35-40

population.description: Patrilineal father-son pairs in the Danish registers with a Danes (individuals of Danish origin); the first generation (grandfathers) is dropped and the father must be identified.
population.ages: Father and son each observed at ages 35-40 (inclusive)
population.selection: Males with father identified, salary observed at ages 35-40, and a country-of-origin group with at least 200 individuals.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in fathers' income ranks within each country-of-origin group; no exogenous shock, reform or instrument is used.

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis is restricted to patrilineal (father-son) descent, so the sample is conditioned on the male line; female labour supply, which is irregular especially among immigrant women, is left out.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a data-construction choice (p. 5); no test is offered.

implies_edges.from: patrilineal father-son line (male descent)

key_assumptions.assumption: Eq. (1) is estimated only for country-of-origin groups with 200 or more individuals, so the sample of groups is conditioned on group size.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated and motivated by precision of the ranking (p. 8; Mogstad et al., 2024).

implies_edges.from: country-of-origin group with 200 or more individuals

key_assumptions.assumption: The average salary observed while father and son are each aged 35-40 is a usable proxy for permanent income, and ranking on it places the two generations on comparable distributions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Motivated in the text by the need to avoid biases related to different fertility decisions across individuals and immigrant groups (p. 6); not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The rank-rank relation is linear within each country-of-origin group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Imposed by the OLS specification of Eq. (1); not tested.

threats_discussed: Statistical uncertainty in the correlates can distort the ranking of groups (Mogstad et al., 2024), addressed with the confidence sets of Chetverikov et al. (2024).
Imposing a three-generation structure under-represents low-income countries (footnote 12, p. 6).
robustness_checks: Ranking rerun at the group level (Figure A2, Appendix), clustering standard errors at country level.
Only the first quartile of the salary distribution (Figure A3, Appendix).
Total income instead of salary (Figure A4, Appendix).
Controlling for the son's education (Figure A5, Appendix).

estimation.specification: Eq. (1): rank-rank regression of the son's income rank on the father's income rank, estimated separately by country of origin; weighted by the number of observations available for each son.
estimation.clustering: Standard errors clustered at father's level (p. 8)
estimation.weights: Each OLS regression is weighted by the number of observations available for each son (p. 8)

source_table.value: Footnote 21, p. 12 (estimates of the Eq. (1) rank-rank slope by group); the ranks of these coefficients are plotted in Fig. 3, p. 9.

evidence.how: Footnote 21 (p. 12) prints the point estimate and the standard error in parentheses only: no stars, no p-value, no confidence interval and no mean or standard deviation of the son's rank.
Both sides of Eq. (1) are income ranks, so the slope is the change in the son's rank per unit change in the father's rank.
The printed estimate 0.22 is 22.0 times its printed standard error (0.01), so the coefficient is far from zero; the footnote itself prints no stars and no p-value.

claims.statement: Among sons cohabiting with a non-Danish partner, the ethnic-capital term interacted with a low income country of origin carries a coefficient of -0.04 relative to Danes.

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark administrative registers; built from the same salary variable (LOENMV) aggregated by country of origin (OPR_LAND / STATSB)

definition.value: Interaction between the ethnic-capital term and the dummy for a low income country of origin, with Danes as the reference group. The text describes Table 6 as re-estimating Eq. (7) 'interacting the variable EC-bar^{co}_{-i} with the groups of the country of origin considered, with Danes as the reference group'; the row label printed in the table is the country average of ln(1 + Salary) interacted with L.

timing.value: Fathers' salaries, averaged by country of origin over the years in which the fathers are aged 35-40

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark administrative registers; variable LOENMV (the paper names the variable but not the register)

definition.value: Natural logarithm of one plus the son's salary, where Salary is the average salary over the years in which the son is aged 35-40 inclusive, computed from LOENMV, deflated to 2019 and converted to US dollars; observations with a value of zero are included.

timing.value: Average over the calendar years in which the son is 35 to 40 years old (inclusive)

units.value: log points of ln(1 + Salary^Son) per unit of the ethnic-capital term, as a difference relative to Danes

estimand.target_population: Father-son pairs in Denmark: sons cohabiting with a non-Danish partner.
estimand.time_horizon: Father and son each observed as the average salary over ages 35-40

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in fathers' salaries and in the country-of-origin average of fathers' salaries; within father's municipality of residence when he is aged 35-40.
